April 16, 2025
Testimony from: Eric H. Bronner, Founder & COO, Veterans for All Voters
To: Maine Joint Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs
RE: Testimony in Support of ME LD 1422, "AN ACT Regarding Open Primary Elections and Ranked-choice Voting"
Mr. Chairman and Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee Members,
My name is Eric Bronner. I'm a Navy veteran, lifelong Independent voter, and the Founder and Chief Operating Officer of Veterans for All Voters--a nonpartisan, nonprofit community of more than 5,000 veterans and supporters from across the country and across the political spectrum. Our mission is to mobilize veterans to advocate for election innovations that unlock competition, reduce polarization, and promote responsive governance.
I'm writing in strong support of LD 1422 because this legislation reflects the core values that veterans like me swore an oath to defend: fairness, accountability, and a government that truly represents "we the people." Veterans for All Voters supported the effort to bring semi-open primaries to Maine. This legislation builds upon Maine's proud tradition of being a national leader in election innovations.
LD 1422 proposes a bold but common-sense reform: allowing all voters--regardless of party affiliation--to participate in a unified primary election, where every candidate appears on the same ballot and the top finishers move on to the general election. Veterans for All Voters agrees with the assessment from the R Street Institute that "there are areas where the bill can and should be improved to better serve voters." Specifically, there is no need for Maine to move backward by not using ranked-choice voting (RCV) in the presidential election; and, adopting a unified, top-four system would increase voter participation, while limiting confusion and administrative complexity.
In the military, leadership isn't given--it's earned. We don't pick leaders based on affiliation or popularity--we choose them based on who can lead effectively and represent the whole team. This bill brings that same spirit of service and accountability to our elections.
Maine has long been a national leader in voting innovation. From pioneering ranked-choice voting to expanding voter access, the state has shown what it means to put voters first. LD 1422 builds on that legacy by creating a process that removes unnecessary barriers, encourages broader participation, and makes elections more competitive and representative.

This reform also speaks directly to the experience of veterans. Nationally, 55% of post-9/11 veterans identify as independent or unaffiliated. Yet in many places - even in states like Maine, with semi-open primaries--they're effectively limited from choosing who appears on the general election ballot--despite paying for those elections with their taxes and, in many cases, their service. Veterans don't ask for special treatment, but we do expect a fair shot. LD 1422 provides that--not just for veterans, but for every Mainer who wants their voice to be fully heard.
By consolidating primaries and leveling the playing field, this legislation will lead to more inclusive campaigns, less toxic partisanship, and outcomes that better reflect the will of the voters. It puts country over party--and that's exactly what our democracy needs right now.
Veterans for All Voters is proud to support LD 1422, and we urge you to pass this legislation. Together, we can strengthen democracy for the next generation--and ensure that every voter in Maine has a fair and equal say.
Thank you for your time and your service to the people of Maine.
Respectfully,
/s/ Eric H. Bronner
Eric H. Bronner Founder & COO Veterans for All Voters eric@veteransforallvoters.org
10044464:
Testimony in Opposition of LD 1422: "An Act Regarding Open Primary Elections and Ranked-choice Voting"
Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and the distinguished members of the Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs, my name is Harris Van Pate, and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free-market think tank, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony in opposition to LD 1422, "An Act Regarding Open Primary Elections and Ranked-choice Voting."
At its core, this bill would significantly alter Maine's electoral process by eliminating party-specific primaries for Governor, U.S. Senate, U.S. House of Representatives, State Senate, and State House races. All candidates--regardless of party enrollment--would appear on a single primary ballot, and all voters--regardless of enrollment--would be able to cast votes in that election.
While proponents may frame this as a move toward greater inclusion and electoral participation, the consequences of such a shift would be deeply harmful to the principles of representative democracy, party integrity, and electoral clarity.
Undermines Political Parties and Voter Choice
Political parties play a critical role in organizing civic participation and representing coherent policy visions. By forcing parties to compete in an open primary with non-members, the bill effectively dilutes their ability to choose their own nominees. Just as no private organization should be compelled to allow outsiders to select its leaders, political parties--recognized by Maine law--deserve the autonomy to determine their own standard-bearers.
This is not a radical position: the U.S. Supreme Court has affirmed the right of political parties to control their nominating processes in cases such as California Democratic Party v. Jones (2000), where it struck down a similar blanket primary law on First Amendment grounds.1 In that case the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that a similar forced open primary law was unconstitutional. This was because forcing political parties to accept non-members in their primaries infringed on their associational rights, since it could dilute the parties' ability to choose candidates who represented their values.
1 https://www.oyez.org/cases/1999/99-401

Further Entrenching Ranked-Choice Voting, a Confusing and Disenfranchising Process
This bill would extend RCV--a deeply flawed system already proven to be problematic in Maine--into even more of our elections. Ranked-choice voting has been shown to increase ballot exhaustion, delay results, and confuse voters. Candidates can be eliminated even if they are the most popular in the first round, and "winners" may not even appear on the "majority" of ballots after rounds of reallocation.
This is not merely hypothetical. In the 2018 2nd Congressional District race, Maine's RCV system overturned the first-round plurality winner.2 That experience fueled distrust and frustration among voters--feelings that this bill would now expand statewide and into general elections for federal offices.
Opens the Door to Strategic Manipulation and Reduces Electoral Clarity
An open, top-two or top-four primary system invites strategic voting and candidate manipulation. Powerful special interests can fund "spoiler" candidates or use vote-splitting tactics to crowd out certain parties from the general election. Worse, voters may be denied a genuine choice between contrasting ideological visions--being instead forced to choose between candidates with marginal differences who do not reflect the full political spectrum.
Rejects the Will of Other States and Voters
The open primary and RCV model is far from widely accepted. In fact, it has faced rejection across the nation. Massachusetts voters resoundingly rejected RCV in 2020,3 and Alaska4 5--the only other state to implement a similar system--now faces a growing movement to repeal it, with a near repeal from last year's ballot, and another voter already scheduled for 2026. Furthermore, thirteen states, such as Idaho, Tennessee, and West Virginia, have banned RCV statewide.6 7 Maine's electoral system should not be an
2 www.npr.org/2018/11/15/668296045/ranked-choice-voting-delivers-another-victory-to-house-democrats 3 https://ballotpedia.org/Massachusetts_Question_2,_Ranked-Choice_Voting_Initiative_(2020) 4 https://ballotpedia.org/Alaska_Ballot_Measure_2,_Repeal_Top-Four_Ranked-Choice_Voting_Initiative_(2024)
5
https://alaskabeacon.com/briefs/new-petition-can-start-signature-gathering-for-repeal-of-ranked-choice-voting-openprimaries-alaska-lt-governor-says/ 6 https://news.ballotpedia.org/2024/07/16/more-states-banned-ranked-choice-voting-in-2024-than-any-other-year/
7
https://news.ballotpedia.org/2025/03/25/thirteen-states-have-now-banned-ranked-choice-voting-as-municipalities-de cide-on-whether-to-adopt-it/

Conclusion
For these reasons, the Maine Policy Institute strongly urges the Committee to vote "Ought Not to Pass" on this legislation. Electoral integrity, clarity, and party self-governance must be preserved if we are to maintain public trust in our democratic institutions. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Veterans and Legal Affairs Committee Testimony in Support of LD1422
Jeremy Gruber, SVP Open Primaries April 16, 2025
Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee-
My name is Jeremy Gruber and I am the Senior Vice President of Open Primaries. Open Primaries is a national non-profit organization dedicated to more open and inclusive election systems. We were leaders of the effort to bring semi-open primaries to Maine. Today Maine's close to 300,000 independent voters can now participate in the state's all important first round of elections. But it's now time to go further.
Like the rest of the country, the state of Maine is facing two hard truths-
First- that independents are the fastest growing group of voters in Maine and the country-they are almost a third of Maine voters and already the largest group of voters nationwide. More and more voters are choosing not to affiliate with a party and
Second-for most races the general election is so uncompetitive, oftentimes to the point of being uncontested-that the primary election is the only election that matters.
Yet in Maine, independent and party voters alike remain siloed in partisan primaries that limit choice, artificially reduce competition and as a result lower voter participation. Why should private political parties determine how Maine's voters run their elections? Primaries are taxpayer funded and government administered. They should fully represent the public.
85% of cities and now four states-Alaska, California, Nebraska (for state legislative races) and Washington use nonpartisan primary elections. No longer are voters siloed. Every voter can choose any candidate in any race and all voters participate equally. You've already voted in a nonpartisan primary-it's how most Maine cities run their elections.
In nonpartisan systems, candidates have to reach out to ALL the voters in order to get elected and stay in office. When you're successful in winning an election where you've had to court all voters-you become a better legislator.

States with nonpartisan primaries are also proving far more immune to the partisan bickering that characterizes so much of our political debates today. They have some of the more productive state legislatures in the country as well.
All the research shows that voter participation goes up in open primaries, but even higher in nonpartisan open primaries. The Bipartisan Policy Center among others issues reports that consistently find that to be the case. When you offer voters real choices at the ballot box, they show up to vote. When less voters get to vote, voting power is distributed unequally.
That's the key to nonpartisan primaries -- empowering voters and elected leaders to work together by removing the structures that keep them apart. Common-sense decision making is in short supply in so many other parts of our country. Nonpartisan primaries help create more space for common sense to flourish.
Nonpartisan primaries will also create real political opportunities for Maine. As my friend David Holt, Mayor of Oklahoma City and Leader of the US Conference of Mayors has said"Nonpartisan open primary systems foster collaboration and bridge building in the service of finding solutions. Closed systems foster zero-sum game competition and partisan rivalry."
Everyone benefits from a healthier, more inclusive political system that encourages competition. That's why nonpartisan primaries are a solution that enjoys broad, bipartisan support among voters.
I urge you to pass LD1422.
Thank you.
Jeremy Gruber jgruber@openprimaries.org (609) 610-1602 www.openprimaries.org

Chairman Hickman, Chairwoman Supica, and members of the committee:
My name is Dr. Jonathan Madison, and I am a governance fellow at the R Street Institute, a nonprofit, nonpartisan public policy research organization. Our mission is to engage in policy analysis and outreach to promote free markets, and limited, effective government in many areas, including election administration. This is why we have an interest in LD 1422.
This bill makes meaningful strides toward improving Maine's electoral systems by requiring all candidates for office to compete in a single primary regardless of party affiliation, with the most voted candidates moving on to the general election. Non-partisan primaries are more inclusive of the general electorate and produce more representative results. This election structure encourages candidates to be more civil in their approach to campaigning.1 Lastly, by advancing the top candidates regardless of partisan affiliation, this approach increases the likelihood that voters will benefit from a competitive race on election day, even in areas where one party is dominant. However, there are areas where the bill can and should be improved to better serve voters.
First, removing presidential elections from ranked choice voting (RCV) is a step backward. Maine has been a national leader in adopting RCV.2 Eliminating RCV for presidential races would be a regression that goes against the opinion of a majority of the state's voters.3 Second, adopting a top-two system for some races while using a top-four system for others would create confusion among voters and administrative complexity. Our research shows that top-four systems offer several advantages over toptwo; they give voters more choices with greater political diversity, reduce vote splitting, and often result

Consumed and concerning LD-1422 by Joe Baldacci, I plead all my innocence in life as I am "not guilty". Ranked Choice Voting is a blessing to Maine and any other state that ratifies. Why do politicians want to abandon this order? - Is my question now. I am registered and on the ballot for "write-in" candidate for Republican Governor of Maine. Now I know why RCV is so precious to democracy. The "people" have not completely felt the pleasure in being inclusive to a General election ballot. Candidates from all over Maine that feel themselves so qualified as to speak with Ethics Commission, register for your favorite office and campaign have some hope that democracy for each one of them will be savory by the shear volume of RCV or Ranked Choice Voting counting procedures at the ballots. Simple to me now; quite good for democracy. When the "people" lose faith in democracy what is there to show they have tried and gained a few votes in the primary election? Candidates get their fair share of the statistics then; and the top candidates are included in the General election to come. I tell you Maine, when the people realize politicians are trying to stop that process of RCV at the ballot, they will eventually realize that a candidate in the future might not get any good votes to show for all the efforts in running a pure, home aid, legitimate campaign in Maine. RCV is precious; thanks senator Joe Balducci. God Bless the cool people of Maine. Sheppard for Governor- the Republican that proves the Democratic party is so historical and true to the state of Maryland to begin a greater Republican party for the rest of America aside from Maine- the state I love as a Republican sophist. Rome has come again; will the senate reveal a provision for anything better than RCV?
10043674:
Susan Bernier South Berwick LD 1422
I oppose LD 1422 "An Act Regarding Open Primary Elections and Ranked-choice Voting."
Everyone votes in the primary using the exact same ballot. All candidates no matter their party/affiliation are listed on the ballot. Using this method means that multiple candidates from the same political party could appear on the general election ballot while other parties may be left off entirely. Imagine that, only candidates from one party advance to the general election ballot?
This system sounds like free-for-all, intended to send a single party to the general election, with Ranked Choice Voting thrown in to further confuse the voter, and provide artificial majorities for some candidates.
I oppose LD 1422 and it "ought not to pass."
